title: SpaceX Plans Consumer Mobile Service That Could Reshape US Wireless Market
excerpt: Elon Musk's SpaceX is considering a Starlink-branded retail mobile service for US consumers, a move that would pit the satellite giant directly against AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile in a market worth over $1.6 trillion.
body:
• SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell told investors the company is considering a Starlink-branded retail mobile service for US consumers, potentially building its own terrestrial wireless network.
  • The move would transform SpaceX from a carrier partner into a direct competitor to AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, which collectively serve nearly 400 million wireless subscribers.
  • SpaceX holds just 65 MHz of spectrum after a $17 billion EchoStar acquisition — a fraction of the 1,020 MHz controlled by the Big Three carriers.
  • The threat has already wiped $46 billion in market value from the three major telecoms, with analysts warning the overhang could persist through 2027.

SpaceX is no longer content to play a supporting role in America's wireless industry. The company is actively exploring a Starlink-branded retail mobile service for US consumers that would put it in direct competition with the country's three dominant carriers, according to the Financial Times.

The proposal, outlined by SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell during investor discussions tied to the company's IPO roadshow, would pair Starlink's constellation of more than 9,600 low-Earth orbit satellites with planned ground-based wireless infrastructure. If executed, it would mark the most aggressive challenge to the US wireless oligopoly in over a decade.

From Partner to Competitor

SpaceX's path to this moment has been years in the making. The company's partnership with T-Mobile, announced in 2022, brought direct-to-cell satellite connectivity to ordinary smartphones — allowing users to send texts and access emergency services in areas without terrestrial coverage. That technology is now live through T-Mobile's T-Satellite service.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=oVhrNGWx0fs

But a retail mobile offering would fundamentally alter the dynamics. "A direct consumer product changes the relationship with the carriers from partner to competitor, and that matters more than the product specs in year one," Roger Entner, founder of telecom research firm Recon Analytics, told Inc.

""SpaceX will disrupt the $1.6T communications industry," Oppenheimer analyst Tim Horan wrote in a client note in June, projecting that Starlink could grow its US customer base to 15 million by 2030."

The financial incentive is clear. Starlink generated close to $3.3 billion in revenue during the first quarter of 2026, accounting for roughly 69 percent of SpaceX's total quarterly revenue. In 2025, Starlink brought in $11.4 billion of SpaceX's $18.7 billion in total revenue and was the company's only profitable segment, according to its IPO prospectus.

The Spectrum Gap and Infrastructure Challenge

Disrupting a $1.6 trillion industry from orbit comes with significant hurdles. The most immediate is spectrum. The three largest US wireless carriers collectively control approximately 1,020 MHz of licensed radio spectrum, according to New Street Research data cited by the Financial Times. SpaceX holds just 65 MHz, acquired through the FCC-approved purchase of EchoStar's wireless spectrum licenses for $17 billion, with an additional $2.6 billion deal completed in November.

That gap limits how much mobile traffic SpaceX could handle, particularly in dense urban areas where spectrum congestion is most acute. Building a competitive terrestrial network would also require billions more in tower infrastructure, fiber backhaul, and retail operations. US wireless providers invested $29 billion in their networks last year alone, according to industry trade group CTIA.

AT&T CFO Pascal Desroches has pushed back on the satellite threat, arguing that existing fiber, cable, and wireless infrastructure covers 99 percent of the US population. Satellite connectivity, he said, is a "great solution" for the remaining 1 percent in very rural areas — but lacks the cost efficiency to compete in suburban and urban markets.

Wall Street Takes Notice

Investors have not waited for clarity. SpaceX's reported ambitions, combined with Bloomberg's report that Charter Communications has held discussions with SpaceX about partnering on a consumer mobile phone, wiped $46 billion in combined market value from Verizon ($20.25 billion), AT&T ($15.74 billion), and T-Mobile ($10.17 billion) within days.

"SpaceX will disrupt the $1.6T communications industry," Oppenheimer analyst Tim Horan wrote in a client note in June, projecting that Starlink could grow its US customer base to 15 million by 2030. The firm identified SpaceX's integrated satellite-and-launch business as a structural advantage that legacy carriers cannot easily replicate.

BNP Paribas analysts cautioned that the "overhang on wireless names around SpaceX may well persist" until two key events resolve: the FCC's Upper C-Band spectrum auction, scheduled for no later than July 2027, and the renewal — or non-renewal — of SpaceX's direct-to-cell deal with T-Mobile.

Carriers Build a Counter-Strategy

The Big Three are not standing still. In May, AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile agreed in principle to form a joint venture aimed at reducing wireless dead zones through satellite-based direct-to-device technology. The carriers want to establish common standards, pool spectrum resources, and share the infrastructure costs of satellite connectivity — effectively collaborating against SpaceX's solo ambitions.

NewStreet Research analyst Blair Levin warned that SpaceX's potential monopoly on satellite launches and low-Earth orbit infrastructure could squeeze traditional providers. The carriers' joint venture appears designed to prevent SpaceX from becoming the sole gatekeeper of satellite-to-phone connectivity.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The ripple effects extend well beyond US borders. SpaceX's push into consumer mobile could accelerate Starlink's global expansion into markets where satellite connectivity fills genuine gaps — including India, where Starlink has long sought regulatory approval. Indian telecom giants Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel, which backs rival satellite operator OneWeb, are already positioning for a satellite broadband contest of their own. A more aggressive SpaceX could intensify that competition. For Indian Americans invested in US telecom stocks or working across the wireless industry, the reshuffling of a $1.6 trillion sector is not a distant concern.

What's Next

Whether SpaceX follows through on Shotwell's proposal remains uncertain. Some analysts, including David Barden of New Street Research, have suggested the move could be a negotiating tactic to extract better revenue terms from existing carrier partners rather than a genuine commitment to building a standalone mobile network.

But the company's trajectory — the spectrum acquisitions, the "Starlink Mobile" trademark filings, the IPO prospectus identifying a $740 billion mobile market opportunity — suggests this is more than posturing. The wireless industry's first new competitive threat in years may be arriving from orbit.
